title: i am an artist in the wild
content:
from my podcast: botanical studies of internet magic
listen on spotify / listen on apple

who gives us the right to call ourselves "artists"? where do you source your sense of legitimacy and validity from? how do you face the voices of imposter syndrome and not-enoughness?

in this episode, we'll unpack the gap between self-perception, other-perception, and the daily process/practice of being an artist. I'll share why claiming yourself as an artist in the wild -- beyond all institutional validation -- is the most powerful thing you can do. you don't owe anyone an explanation.

the struggle to call ourselves artists

Recently, I had a discussion inside Labyrinth Library about why it's so hard to call ourselves artists or writers when we introduce ourselves. I want to untangle this dynamic of why we feel the need to make ourselves legible, and what it means to claim and inhabit ourselves as artists undomesticated by society—living in the wild.

Ultimately, it's about claiming our right as artists to not only exist and survive, but also to thrive. We'll explore the gap between how other people see us and how we see ourselves, and how much we let other people's perceptions affect our sense of self-worth.

my personal journey

I worked my last part-time job at a graphic design studio in 2018 and started calling myself an artist in 2019. Of course, I struggled with feeling unvalidated by institutions. It took me more than a year of deep existential suffering to recognize that for me, being an artist means I make art, I take it seriously, and I will survive. Period.

But whenever I introduced myself as an artist or writer, I could anticipate the thoughts popping up in the other person's mind. There were the survival questions—but how do you pay the bills? How do you eat? How do you live in New York City? Do you have rich parents? And then the legitimacy questions—do you show your work at galleries? Are you in any museums? Did you publish any books I've heard of? Are you really an artist or just calling yourself one? Are you a hobbyist? Are you good enough to call yourself an artist?

Even when they didn't say these questions out loud, my mind would announce them in my head, triggering an existential spiral.

question of being legible

When we introduce ourselves, several things happen. How do I describe myself in a way that makes sense to your worldview? Do I feel the need to defend myself? Do I feel the need to hide what I am? Do I need to be a closet artist?

The difference is striking—introducing yourself as a product manager doesn't incite shame or justification or self-consciousness. There's no need to prove yourself as a good enough product manager.

being an artist in the wild

To claim yourself as an artist is to announce to the world that you are undomesticated. You are free from the tethers of societal boxes. Especially without institutional affiliation—without being published by this or that house, without a teaching job or grant or fellowship—you lose the sense of validity and legibility to others.

But here's the reframe: This means you are an artist in the wild. And your only obligation is to survive in the wild.

When you claim yourself as an artist outside institutions, you break all the rules of what others believe is possible. There's an assumption that you must have a rich partner or privileged family, that you must have a day job, that art is a luxury or hobby. How dare you call yourself an artist and survive in the wild?

But being an artist in the wild means: I am an artist because it is the way I exist and inhabit my body, my life in this world. It happens to be in the wild because I don't need recognition or validation to continue doing the work that is my art.

When others hear this, there's an instinct to devalue the wild, to feel existential terror. If someone can survive without institutional backing, what's keeping them from doing the same? Seeing someone else in the wild triggers fear: If they can survive, then what's keeping me from surviving?

Three Principles

1. Being an Artist is About Practice and Process, Not Performance

The work of being an artist is not about performing an identity or earning the right to call yourself an artist. It's about practice and process.

We can always set criteria that keep getting higher—boxes to check, thinking "I'll be a real artist when I..." Even if you make the New York Times bestseller list or get featured in a magazine, you can still have imposter syndrome. This if/then thinking is a trap.

For me, being an artist means I don't need to pay my bills by selling paintings, nor do I need to reject money and be poor to earn the right. It means I'm devoted to my artistic practice—it's not a luxury or hobby, it's a necessity, it's why I'm alive. It's both the gift I have to offer and what makes life bearable, beautiful, and meaningful.

From this grounding, I put deep energy into practice, process, and systems to commit to my art.

You can call yourself an artist, others can call you an artist, but when you truly feel like an artist, it's about how you inhabit your creative, physical, and energetic body in the day to day.

2. You Don't Owe Anyone an Explanation

It is not your job to make what you do legible to others, to stretch other people's imaginations of what's possible, or to be responsible for how they see you. Making them see you as an artist won't grant you authority to feel like an artist.

Yes, to be an artist is to be interesting, unconventional, and different. You can claim it. You can make a practice of introducing yourself as an artist—say "I'm an artist, period"—and use it as mindfulness practice. Notice: Do I feel the urge to defend? Do I feel fraud or imposter syndrome? Do I feel anxiety spiraling?

Sometimes all that anxiety is self-imposed. Sometimes the other party is just a well-meaning, curious stranger. They're not judging you—we're judging ourselves.

But also, sometimes in certain environments, I just don't feel like talking. In those cases, I introduce myself in the most boring way possible. When they ask what I do, I say "I build websites"—which is technically true, and it's a verb, not a noun.

Other people can think whatever they want about me, and it doesn't change how I relate to myself.

Let me tell you—what I just said is so hard. I can't tell you how many years I struggled to call myself an artist, felt extremely defensive, felt anxiety, felt imposter syndrome.

The practice is about cultivating boundaries and containment. You don't have to tell people what you are. You can just be what you are. You don't need anyone to validate who you are in order to be yourself.

3 — Artists Have the Right to Survive and Thrive

I used to compartmentalize the part of myself that made money from the part that was an artist. Unconsciously, I thought there was an adult me (the business side) and the artist me was like a child. I would make money from designing websites and teaching, then make art for nourishing my soul and pleasure.

Because it took me so long to come to terms with myself as an artist, I didn't want money or business to contaminate that. I protected being an artist as if it was a princess in an ivory tower. At the same time, I resented having to make money and felt ashamed about not having much money when friends worked corporate jobs.

A few years ago, I had a huge breakthrough: This compartmentalization was not serving me—it was hindering my power.

I realized that being an artist is about a process, practice, and sensibility of vision that can be applied to any domain. To be an artist is to bring vision, wild imagination, a sense of possibility, and generative creative power to everything you do, to anything you touch.

You're like the Empress—you walk through a garden and all the flowers bloom. There can be feasts everywhere.

I believe that as an artist, you have a right to abundance. This can be hard to imagine in how our society is structured, but as artists, we already are abundant. The work is materializing that abundance into the world—creating resources with our power for the world, not needing art to be a sacred thing that could be easily poisoned.

Our art is stronger than that. It can be accessible, shared, and expansive. We can allow ourselves to receive energy, reciprocity, recognition, and money for what we offer the world.

claiming your right to exist

As an artist in the wild, it's about claiming the right to exist, claiming your worthiness, and claiming your abundance.

I feel on fire when I talk about this because I've grappled with money, worthiness, and validation—especially growing up in a status-obsessed Chinese immigrant family environment where I was told that if I became an artist, I would starve.

I'm not starving right now. I'm thriving.

My art is integrated and interwoven into all the courses I teach, the community I lead, the website worlds I build. Any business projects are an expression of my artist self. It's not contained to my outputs—it is the texture of the way I touch and engage with the world.

It's the way I metabolize life and deep feeling into something other people can experience and be part of.

closing thoughts

You claim and inhabit your identity as an artist in the day to day. You are an artist because art is your life, art is your practice, art is your process.

You are not responsible for how other people see you or don't see you. You don't need justification to be what you are. Your self-perception is what matters most.

And of course, this is so hard. Sometimes you'll feel spirally, existential, full of imposter syndrome. This is part of the practice.

In those moments, return to the work. Return to what matters most to you. Do the things that make you feel—in your bones, in your blood, in your body—that you are an artist.
